chapterNote: Chapter 15 gathers a cluster of antithetic proverbs around two great themes: the power of the tongue and the all-seeing presence of the LORD. The chapter opens and closes on speech (vv. 1-2, 4, 7, 23, 26, 28) and is anchored at its center by the watching eyes of God (v. 3), who weighs sacrifice and prayer (vv. 8-9, 29), reads the hidden heart (v. 11), and topples the proud while securing the lowly (v. 25). The recurring contrast is the soft word against the harsh, the glad heart against the broken spirit, and 'better a little with the fear of the LORD' than great wealth with trouble (v. 16) — closing, fittingly, where the book began: the fear of the LORD as the school of wisdom, with humility going before honor (v. 33).

1.text: A gentle answer turns wrath aside, but a cutting word stirs anger up.
1.amp: A soft [rak — tender, yielding, gentle] answer turns away [shub — causes to turn back, sends home] wrath [chemah — hot fury, like a poison rising], but a painful [etsev — grievous, full of toil and hurt] word stirs up [alah — makes anger climb, ascend like flame] anger [aph — the flaring nostril, hot displeasure].
1.notes: shub (H7725) is the great 'return' verb — the soft word literally makes wrath turn around and go back where it came; chemah (H2534) is heat/fury, while aph (H639) pictures anger in the flared nostril. The proverb is itself an instance of its own counsel: gentleness defuses, harshness inflames.

2.text: The tongue of the wise makes knowledge good to hear, but the mouth of fools gushes folly out.
2.amp: The tongue [lashon] of the wise [chakam — skilled, discerning] handles knowledge [daat] well [yatab — makes it good, pleasing, fitting], but the mouth [peh] of fools [kesil — the dullard who will not learn] pours out [naba — bubbles, belches, spews] folly [ivvelet].
2.notes: yatab (H3190) means to make good or do well — the wise serve truth in a form that goes down well, rightly seasoned. naba (H5042), to bubble up or gush, is comically vivid: the fool's mouth is a spring that cannot hold back its own foolishness (cf. v. 28; Prov 12:23).

3.text: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch over the evil and the good.
3.amp: The eyes [ayin] of the LORD [YHWH] are in every place [maqom — every standing-spot, every locale], keeping watch [tsaphah — standing sentry, the watchman on the wall] over the evil [ra] and the good [tov].
3.notes: tsaphah (H6822) is the watchman's vigilant looking (cf. Ezek 3:17) — God is not a distant overseer but an ever-present sentinel. Set at the chapter's heart, this verse undergirds every other: speech, sacrifice, and the secret heart are all lived out under the unblinking gaze of the LORD (cf. Prov 5:21; 2 Chr 16:9).

4.text: A tongue that heals is a tree of life, but a twisted tongue breaks the spirit.
4.amp: A healing [marpe — soundness, a cure, restoration] tongue [lashon] is a tree [ets] of life [chay], but perverseness [selef — crookedness, distortion] in it is a breaking [sheber — a fracture, a shattering] of the spirit [ruach].
4.notes: marpe (H4832) is medicine, healing — the literal Hebrew is 'the healing of the tongue' (so the KJV margin). Set against it is sheber (H7667), a fracture or wreck; the same tongue that can be a tree of life (echoing Gen 2-3; Prov 3:18) can also crush the breath out of a person.

5.text: A fool spurns his father's correction, but whoever takes a rebuke to heart grows shrewd.
5.amp: A fool [evil — the morally thick, contemptuous of instruction] despises [naats — spurns, treats with scorn] his father's [ab] correction [musar — formative discipline], but he who guards [shamar — keeps, treasures, watches over] reproof [tokachat] becomes prudent [aram — gains shrewd good sense].
5.notes: naats (H5006) is contempt — the fool does not merely ignore musar (H4148) but sneers at it. Over against him, shamar (H8104), to keep/guard, treats reproof as something precious worth protecting; the result is aram (H6191), the shrewd practical wisdom that knows how to live (cf. Prov 1:8; 13:1).

6.text: In the house of the righteous is abundant treasure, but the income of the wicked brings ruin.
6.amp: In the house [bayit] of the righteous [tsaddiq — the one in right standing] is great [rav — abundant] treasure [chosen — stored-up wealth, reserves of strength], but in the revenue [tebuah — the harvest, the produce] of the wicked [rasha — the guilty law-breaker] is trouble [akar — what is stirred up muddy, what brings disaster].
6.notes: chosen (H2633) is stored wealth that doubles as strength; the contrast is not amount but character — the wicked may have income (tebuah, H8393), but it comes already troubled. akar (H5916) is to stir up and bring calamity (cf. Achan, Josh 7:25); their very gain carries ruin folded inside it.

7.text: The lips of the wise scatter knowledge like good seed; the heart of fools is not so.
7.amp: The lips [saphah] of the wise [chakam] disperse [zarah — scatter abroad, winnow] knowledge [daat], but the heart [leb] of fools [kesil] is not so.
7.notes: zarah (H2219) is to scatter or winnow — the wise sow knowledge broadcast like a farmer flinging seed, and in winnowing they separate the worthwhile from the chaff. The pointed contrast moves from the wise man's lips to the fool's heart: the problem is not merely the fool's mouth but the empty source behind it (cf. v. 2; Luke 6:45).

8.text: The LORD detests the sacrifice of the wicked, but the prayer of the upright is His delight.
8.amp: The sacrifice [zebach — the slaughtered offering] of the wicked [rasha] is an abomination [toevah — a thing loathed, repugnant] to the LORD [YHWH], but the prayer [tephillah] of the upright [yashar — the straight, the level] is His delight [ratson — His favor, His glad acceptance].
8.notes: toevah (H8441) is the strongest word for what God finds detestable; ratson (H7522) is His good pleasure and acceptance. The proverb cuts to the heart of true religion: God weighs the worshiper, not merely the gift — ritual from a crooked life repels Him, while the bare prayer of the upright delights Him (cf. 1 Sam 15:22; Isa 1:11-15).

9.text: The LORD detests the way of the wicked, but He loves the one who chases after righteousness.
9.amp: The way [derek — the road, the whole manner of life] of the wicked [rasha] is an abomination [toevah] to the LORD [YHWH], but He loves [ahab] him who pursues [radaph — chases, runs hard after] righteousness [tsedaqah].
9.notes: radaph (H7291) is the verb for hot pursuit, even hunting down — the same energy a wicked man spends on plunder, the righteous spend chasing tsedaqah (H6666). Paired with v. 8, the two verses move from worship to walk: the LORD weighs both the altar and the road, and what He loves is not arrival but the pursuit (cf. 1 Tim 6:11).

10.text: Stern discipline waits for the one who deserts the path, and whoever hates correction will die.
10.amp: Correction [musar — discipline] is grievous [ra — harsh, hard, painful] for him who forsakes [azab — abandons, lets go of] the way [orach — the well-trodden path], and he who hates [sane — holds in hostile aversion] reproof [tokachat] shall die [mut].
10.notes: the discipline is grievous (ra, H7451) not because it is cruel but because the deserter feels its sting precisely as he leaves the path (orach, H734). The escalation is fatal: to hate (sane, H8130) reproof is to refuse the very thing that turns a man back from death (cf. Prov 5:23; 10:17).

11.text: Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD — how much more, then, the hearts of mortals.
11.amp: Sheol [sheol — the grave, the realm of the dead] and Destruction [abaddon — the abyss, the place of ruin] are before the LORD [YHWH] — how much more, then, the hearts [leb] of the children [ben] of men [adam — mankind, the sons of Adam]?
11.notes: sheol (H7585) and abaddon (H11) are the deepest, most hidden places imaginable — the underworld lies bare to God. The argument runs from greater to lesser: if the abyss hides nothing from Him, the human heart hides far less (cf. v. 3; Heb 4:13; Ps 139:8). The all-seeing eyes of v. 3 reach even into Sheol.

12.text: A scoffer has no love for one who corrects him; he will not go near the wise.
12.amp: A scorner [luts — the mocker who sneers at what is sacred] does not love [ahab] one who reproves [yakach — one who argues, convicts, sets right] him; to the wise [chakam] he will not go [yalak — he will not walk, will not draw near].
12.notes: the luts (H3887), the scoffer, is the most hardened of Proverbs' three fool-types — not merely ignorant but defiant. yakach (H3198) is to reprove with reasoned conviction; the scoffer's tell is that he steers clear (yalak, H3212) of the wise entirely, lest he be corrected (cf. Prov 9:7-8; 13:1).

13.text: A glad heart lights up the face, but heartache crushes the spirit within.
13.amp: A joyful [sameach — merry, rejoicing] heart [leb] makes the face [panim — the countenance] cheerful [yatab — good, bright, well], but by sorrow [atstsebeth — ache, grief, a wound] of the heart [leb] the spirit [ruach] is broken [nake — struck down, stricken, made contrite].
13.notes: yatab (H3190), the same 'make good' verb as in v. 2, here brightens the panim (H6440) — the inner gladness surfaces on the face. Its opposite, atstsebeth (H6094), is a deep ache that does not stay hidden either: it breaks the ruach (H7307), the very breath of life (cf. v. 15; Prov 17:22).

14.text: The discerning heart goes seeking knowledge, but the mouth of fools grazes on folly.
14.amp: The heart [leb] of the discerning [biyn — the one who perceives, who tells things apart] seeks [baqash — searches out, pursues] knowledge [daat], but the mouth [peh] of fools [kesil] feeds [raah — shepherds itself, grazes, pastures] on folly [ivvelet].
14.notes: baqash (H1245) is active searching — the wise heart is hungry for daat and goes hunting it. The contrast is in the verb raah (H7462), 'to pasture': the fool does not search, he merely grazes, idly chewing the folly nearest at hand (cf. v. 2; Hos 12:1).

15.text: Every day is grim for the afflicted, but a cheerful heart keeps a feast that never ends.
15.amp: All the days [yom] of the afflicted [ani — the bowed-down, the poor and oppressed] are evil [ra — wretched, hard], but he of a good [tov — glad, well-favored] heart [leb] has a continual [tamid — perpetual, unbroken] feast [mishteh — a banquet].
15.notes: the proverb relocates the feast from the table to the heart: tamid (H8548) is the word for the perpetual offering, the unceasing flame — so the glad heart keeps an unbroken banquet whatever the outward want. ani (H6041), the afflicted, may not lack bread so much as joy; the cure is not circumstance but a heart made tov (cf. v. 13; Prov 17:1).

16.text: Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great wealth with turmoil along with it.
16.amp: Better [tov] is a little [meat — a small amount] with the fear [yirah — reverent awe] of the LORD [YHWH], than great [rav — abundant] treasure [otsar — a storehouse of riches] and turmoil [mehumah — panic, confusion, uproar] with it.
16.notes: the first of the chapter's 'better' sayings weighs quantity against quality: a little (meat, H4592) under yirat YHWH (H3374 + H3068) outweighs a full treasury (otsar, H214) churning with mehumah (H4103), the dread and disorder that haunt ill-founded wealth (cf. v. 17; Ps 37:16; 1 Tim 6:6).

17.text: Better a meal of vegetables where love is than a fattened ox served with hatred.
17.amp: Better [tov] is a portion [aruchah — an allotted meal] of herbs [yaraq — green vegetables] where love [ahabah] is, than a fattened [abas — stall-fed, grain-fattened] ox [shor] and hatred [sinah] with it.
17.notes: the second 'better' saying narrows v. 16 to the table: a poor man's bowl of greens (yaraq, H3419) seasoned with ahabah (H160) beats a rich man's prize ox where sinah (H8135), hatred, sits at the board. The proverb prizes the company over the cuisine — love is the true delicacy (cf. v. 16; Prov 17:1).

18.text: A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but the patient one quiets a quarrel.
18.amp: A wrathful [chemah — hot-fury] man [ish] stirs up [garah — excites, provokes, sets contending] strife [madon — contention, discord], but he who is slow [arek — long, patient] to anger [aph] quiets [shaqat — stills, brings to rest] a quarrel [riyb — a dispute, a legal contention].
18.notes: arek aph (H750 + H639), 'long of nostril,' is the Hebrew idiom for patience — it is one of God's own self-descriptions (Exod 34:6). The chapter's bookend with v. 1 is plain: chemah ignites, patience extinguishes; shaqat (H8252) is the verb for a land at rest after war (cf. Prov 29:22).

19.text: The sluggard's road is hedged with thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway.
19.amp: The way [derek] of the sluggard [atsel — the lazy man] is like a hedge [mesukah — a barricade, a thorn-fence] of thorns [chedeq — briars, prickly growth], but the path [orach] of the upright [yashar — the straight] is built up [salal — raised, banked, made into a highway].
19.notes: salal (H5549) is to cast up a road — to raise a graded causeway (KJV margin: 'a causey'). The sluggard's laziness makes every step feel like fighting through briars (chedeq, H2336), while uprightness clears and grades the road ahead. The obstacles are largely of the lazy man's own imagining (cf. Prov 22:13; 26:13).

20.text: A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish man treats his mother with contempt.
20.amp: A wise [chakam] son [ben] makes a father [ab] glad [samach — rejoice], but a foolish [kesil] man [adam] despises [bazah — holds in contempt, treats as worthless] his mother [em].
20.notes: the proverb deliberately echoes 10:1, framing this section of the book. bazah (H959) is to regard as worthless — the fool's sin against his mother is not active cruelty so much as cold contempt. Father's gladness and mother's grief are set as the twin measures of a son's wisdom or folly (cf. v. 5; Prov 23:24-25).

21.text: Folly delights the one with no sense, but a man of understanding walks a straight road.
21.amp: Folly [ivvelet] is joy [simchah — gladness, celebration] to him who lacks [chaser — is void of, destitute of] heart [leb — here, sense and judgment], but a man [ish] of understanding [tebunah — discernment] makes his walk [yalak] straight [yashar — right, level].
21.notes: to be 'void of heart' (chaser leb, literally lacking leb, H3820) is the Hebrew idiom for having no sense (so the KJV margin). The fool finds his folly a party (simchah, H8057), while the man of tebunah (H8394) keeps his steps yashar — straight and on the line. Wisdom is steady walking, not the giddy thrill of folly (cf. v. 14; Prov 10:23; Eph 5:15).

22.text: Plans fall apart for lack of counsel, but with many counselors they stand firm.
22.amp: Without counsel [sod — a deliberating council, a confidential conference] purposes [machashabah — plans, thought-out designs] are frustrated [parar — broken, annulled, brought to nothing], but in the multitude [rov — abundance] of counselors [yaats — advisers] they are established [qum — raised up, made to stand].
22.notes: sod (H5475) is the closed circle of trusted advisers taking counsel together; machashabah (H4284) is a carefully devised plan. Without the council the plan is parar (H6565), broken off; with many yaats (H3289) it is qum (H6965), made to stand. Wisdom is communal, not solitary (cf. Prov 11:14; 24:6).

23.text: A man finds joy in giving a fitting reply — and how good is a word at the right time!
23.amp: A man [ish] has joy [simchah] in the answer [maaneh — the fitting response, the reply] of his mouth [peh], and a word [dabar] in its season [et — its right time, its appointed moment] — how good [tov] it is!
23.notes: et (H6256) is the appointed, ripe moment — the same word as Ecclesiastes' 'time for everything.' The proverb celebrates not just a true word but a timely one: a maaneh (H4617) spoken at the right et is doubly tov, a joy to the speaker and a gift to the hearer (cf. Prov 25:11; Isa 50:4).

24.text: For the wise the path of life runs upward, that he may turn away from Sheol below.
24.amp: The way [orach] of life [chay] leads upward [maal — above, on high] for the wise [sakal — the prudent, the one who acts with insight], that he may turn aside [sur — depart, swerve away] from Sheol [sheol — the grave] beneath [mattah — below, downward].
24.notes: the proverb pictures two directions on one road: maal (H4605), upward, and mattah (H4295), downward. sakal (H7919) is insight that produces success — such a man's life climbs toward God and away from the descending pull of sheol (H7585). The geography is moral: wisdom is an ascent, folly a descent (cf. Prov 2:18-19; Col 3:1-2).

25.text: The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but He secures the widow's boundary stones.
25.amp: The LORD [YHWH] will pull down [nasach — uproot, tear away] the house [bayit] of the proud [geeh — the arrogant, the high-and-lifted-up], but He will set firm [natsab — establish, make to stand] the boundary [gebul — the border, the property line] of the widow [almanah].
25.notes: nasach (H5255) is to pluck up by the roots — the proud man's whole house is torn out of the ground. The contrast is tender: God Himself stands as kinsman-defender for the almanah (H490), fixing the gebul (H1366) — the landmark stone that the powerful loved to move (Deut 19:14; Prov 23:10). He topples the high and guards the lowly (cf. v. 33; Luke 1:52).

26.text: The LORD detests the schemes of the wicked, but gracious words are pure in His sight.
26.amp: The thoughts [machashabah — plots, devices] of the wicked [ra] are an abomination [toevah] to the LORD [YHWH], but the words [emer] of the pure [tahor — clean, undefiled] are pleasant [naim — lovely, delightful].
26.notes: machashabah (H4284), the same 'plans' word as v. 22, here turns sinister — the wicked man's inner schemes are toevah (H8441), loathsome to God. But pleasant words (the literal Hebrew is 'words of pleasantness,' naim, H5278) rise pure (tahor, H2889) before Him. As in vv. 3 and 11, God reads the heart behind the speech (cf. Prov 16:2).

27.text: Whoever grasps for dishonest gain wrecks his own household, but the one who hates bribes will live.
27.amp: He who is greedy [batsa — cuts off gain by violence, grasps unjustly] for gain [betsa — ill-gotten profit] troubles [akar — brings disaster on, stirs to ruin] his own house [bayit], but he who hates [sane] bribes [mattanah — gifts given to corrupt] shall live [chayah — have life, be revived].
27.notes: betsa (H1215) is profit gotten by violence or fraud — the same root that drove the gang in 1:19. akar (H5916), the 'trouble' verb of v. 6, returns: greed poisons a man's own bayit. To hate corrupting gifts (mattanah, H4979) is to choose life (chayah, H2421) over loot (cf. Exod 23:8; 1 Tim 6:9-10).

28.text: The heart of the righteous weighs how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked spews out evil.
28.amp: The heart [leb] of the righteous [tsaddiq] ponders [hagah — muses, mutters over, weighs deeply] to answer [anah — to respond], but the mouth [peh] of the wicked [rasha] pours out [naba — gushes, spews] evil things [ra].
28.notes: hagah (H1897) is to murmur and meditate — the same word for meditating on the Law day and night (Ps 1:2); the righteous chew on a reply before giving it. Against this measured thought, naba (H5042), the 'gush/belch' verb of v. 2, marks the wicked: they spill evil without a moment's weighing (cf. v. 14; Matt 12:34).

29.text: The LORD keeps His distance from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous.
29.amp: The LORD [YHWH] is far [rachoq — distant, removed] from the wicked [rasha], but He hears [shama — listens to, heeds] the prayer [tephillah] of the righteous [tsaddiq].
29.notes: shama (H8085) is not bare hearing but attentive, responsive listening — the same verb as 'hear, O Israel.' Picking up v. 8, the proverb sets nearness against distance: the wicked find God rachoq (H7350), withdrawn; the righteous find their tephillah (H8605) welcomed and answered (cf. Ps 34:15-18; John 9:31).

30.text: A bright-eyed look gladdens the heart, and good news puts marrow in the bones.
30.amp: The light [maor — brightness, radiance] of the eyes [ayin] rejoices [samach] the heart [leb], and a good [tov] report [shemuah — news, tidings] makes the bones [etsem] fat [dashen — enriches, refreshes, makes them flourish].
30.notes: dashen (H1878) is to make fat in the good Hebrew sense — to give vigor and abundance to the very etsem (H6106), the bones, the frame of one's strength. Whether maor (H3974) means a bright glance from another or the sparkle of one's own restored eyes, good tidings (shemuah, H8052) are felt bodily, down to the marrow (cf. v. 13; Prov 16:24; 17:22).

31.text: The ear that heeds life-giving correction will make its home among the wise.
31.amp: The ear [ozen] that hears [shama — listens, heeds] the reproof [tokachat] of life [chay] will lodge [lun — spend the night, dwell, abide] among [qereb — in the midst, in the inner circle] the wise [chakam].
31.notes: lun (H3885) is to lodge or spend the night — the listening ear does not merely visit wisdom but takes up residence in its qereb (H7130), its inner company. There is a 'reproof of life' (tokachat, H8433): correction that, far from killing, leads to life and to a permanent place among the wise (cf. v. 32; Prov 13:18; 25:12).

32.text: Whoever refuses correction despises his own soul, but the one who heeds reproof gains good sense.
32.amp: He who refuses [para — lets go, casts off, runs loose from] correction [musar] despises [maas — rejects, spurns] his own soul [nephesh], but he who hears [shama] reproof [tokachat] gets [qanah — acquires, buys, gains] understanding [leb — a sound heart, good sense].
32.notes: para (H6544) is to let loose or throw off restraint — to refuse musar is to abandon oneself. Such a man maas (H3988), rejects, his own nephesh (H5315); but listening literally 'possesses a heart' (qanah leb, H7069 + H3820, so the KJV margin) — correction is the price one pays to acquire understanding (cf. v. 31; Prov 19:8).

33.text: The fear of the LORD is wisdom's discipline, and humility comes before honor.
33.amp: The fear [yirah — reverent awe] of the LORD [YHWH] is the instruction [musar — the discipline, the formative training] of wisdom [chokmah], and before [panim — in front of, going ahead of] honor [kabod — weight, glory] is humility [anavah — lowliness, meekness].
33.notes: the chapter closes where the book opened (1:7): yirat YHWH (H3374 + H3068) is the school of chokmah (H2451), the discipline (musar, H4148) that shapes a wise life. The second line states the order God honors — anavah (H6038), humility, walks ahead of kabod (H3519), glory. The way up is down (cf. v. 25; Prov 18:12; 22:4; Jas 4:10).
